14.content: Development builds throw for a next state that holds a circular reference, an object that holds itself through its values, which Mutative does not support; see Shared references. Production builds skip this check.

16.content: Freezing visits every object that is not frozen yet, so it costs time on every update, most of all for states that change wide objects or large arrays. In the benchmark, Immer, which freezes by default, took longer with auto-freeze than without it in most of the selected workloads, and Mutative's defaults leave it off.

17.content: Enable auto-freeze in development to catch accidental changes to the state, and leave it off in production for speed: `makeCreator({ enableAutoFreeze: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' })`. Keep it on in production if other code relies on a frozen state.

42.content: By default, Mutative drafts plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, and leaves every other value as it is: a class instance, a `Date` or an object without a prototype in the state is shared by the draft, the base state and the next state. The `mark` option changes that for the values you choose, without changing the values or their classes.

43.content: A mark is a function that receives each value that a recipe reads from a draft, and `{ mutable: 'mutable', immutable: 'immutable' }`. It returns:

44.content: `'immutable'` to draft the value, such as a class instance. Mutative copies it when the recipe changes it, keeping its prototype.

45.content: `'mutable'` to keep the value out of drafts. The recipe reads and changes the value itself, and every value that it holds, and the next state shares it.

46.content: A function that returns a shallow copy of the value, to draft it with that copy.

47.content: Nothing, to draft the value as usual.

48.content: Pass a list of marks to combine them: the first one that returns a value decides, as in `mark: [markSimpleObject, markTodos]`. `markSimpleObject()` is a mark for objects without a prototype and plain objects of other realms.

51.content: A mark that returns a copy function cannot be combined with patches or auto-freeze, which development builds report with an error, and some patches might not apply to such values.

52.content: In strict mode, reading a value marked `mutable` from a draft throws outside `unsafe()`, as reading any value that is not drafted does.

54.content: The first read of such a value returns its copy itself, and later reads return a draft of the copy. Changes through either reach the next state, but the methods of a `Date`, and of other objects that keep their data in internal slots or private fields, work only on the copy itself, so read such a value once and change it through that reference, as the recipe above does. To change a `Date` without a mark, assign a new one instead.

55.content: Mutative copies an instance that `mark` makes `immutable` with all its own properties, non-enumerable ones included, and reads its own accessors as values, as Immer's `setUseStrictShallowCopy('class_only')` does. To copy quickly, it assigns the own properties that are enumerable, writable and configurable instead of defining them, as Immer's default copy does. An own property that shadows a setter of its class, such as a class field over an accessor of a base class, therefore runs that setter on the copy, which can change objects that the copy shares with the base state, and one that shadows a getter without a setter or a read-only property makes the copy throw. Keep such values in accessors of the class or under other keys.

65.content: Mutative v2 keeps the v1 API. The changes below, made since v1.3.0, can affect existing code.

66.content: **ES2018 output.** Every build targets ES2018 instead of ES2015, so object spread stays native. Engines that support Proxy but not ES2018 syntax, such as Chrome 49–59, Firefox 18–54, Safari 10–11.0 and Edge 12–18, need Mutative transpiled by your build.

67.content: **Bundlers.** The ESM entry compares `process.env.NODE_ENV` at each development check instead of always running development code. Production bundles, in which the bundler defines `NODE_ENV` as `production`, drop the development checks and warnings and throw minified errors, as CommonJS consumers already did. Bundles that target Node.js without defining `NODE_ENV`, such as esbuild with `platform: 'node'`, now include both CommonJS builds; define `NODE_ENV` or keep Mutative external.

68.content: **Node.js ESM.** In Node.js, `import` resolves a module that re-exports the CommonJS build, so `import` and `require` share one instance and both follow `NODE_ENV`. Previously, `import` always ran the development ESM build as a separate instance.

69.content: **Browsers without a bundler.** `dist/mutative.esm.mjs` and `dist/mutative.esm.js` read `process.env.NODE_ENV`, so a page that loads them directly, for example from a raw CDN URL, fails with `process is not defined`. Load `dist/mutative.esm.production.min.mjs` instead, or the UMD build that the `unpkg` and `jsdelivr` fields point to.

70.content: **Production errors.** Production builds throw `Minified Mutative error #<code>` with a link to the errors page instead of the full message, also for `apply()`, `original()` and `rawReturn()`. Development builds keep the messages. Code that matches error messages in production must match the codes instead.

71.content: **Order.** The patches of a nested draft now come before those of its parents, the order Immer uses. For example, `const item = draft.list[0]; draft.list.length = 0; item.text = 'b'; draft.item = item;` yields the `list` length replace before the `item` add. Applying the patches gives the same state as before, and replace patches that only restated an unchanged draft at its original index are no longer emitted.

72.content: **Values.** A patch value that was a draft is now the object that the next state holds instead of a deep copy, and it is frozen with the state when `enableAutoFreeze` is on. `apply()` still copies patch values before applying them. Copy a patch value before mutating it.

73.content: **Moved drafts.** A changed draft that leaves its key, because `sort()` or an assignment moved it or another value replaced it there, no longer emits patches under its old path; the patches of its parent carry its value. In v1, the patches of such a recipe could fail to apply, for example the inverse patches once a primitive took the old key.

74.content: **Set items.** A changed item of a Set that also added or removed items is carried by the Set's `remove` and `add` patches. v1 also emitted patches under the item's position in the changed Set, which replay applied to whatever sat at that position in the base Set, or could not apply at all. A Set that only changed its items keeps the patches under each item's position.

75.content: **Original objects assigned over drafts.** Assigning the original object of a draft to the key that holds the draft is recorded like any other assignment: when the draft was read at that key, the key holds its original value again and emits no patch; when the draft was moved there from another key, the key emits the patch of that assignment. In v1, both cases emitted a `remove` patch for an object key that the state kept, and the second emitted no patch for an array element, so replaying the patches dropped the key or lost the element.

76.content: `shift`, `unshift`, `splice` and `reverse` run natively on the draft's copy of a plain array, and `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf` and `includes` search it natively; see which array methods run natively. For data arrays, the results are those of v1 and the patches replay in both directions. An accessor property on an array index is read as a data value, so its getter may run a different number of times.

77.content: `current()` of a changed array copies the current array instead of reading every element through the draft. Base elements that a native method moved and that hold drafts of an outer `create()` call are left as they are, as unmoved elements always were.

78.content: To search a large array without drafting each element it visits, search `current(draft.list)` and change the match through the draft; see `current()`.

79.content: With `enableAutoFreeze`, production builds no longer search frozen objects in a value returned from a recipe, the returned value included, or the values they hold, for drafts, and leave a draft there unresolved. Development builds still search them and throw when they find one, also in an unfrozen object that a frozen one holds, where v1 replaced it. Never put a draft in a frozen object or in a value it holds. Without auto-freeze, returned values are searched as in v1.

80.content: In strict mode, development builds warn once when a recipe leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged, as a search through a large draft array does.

81.content: In strict mode, `rawReturn()` of a value without drafts no longer prints contradictory warnings.

82.content: With `enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }`, development builds throw when a patch path would hold a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key, as a string path cannot name such a key: applying the patch writes another key, for example `'1'` instead of `1`, or fails for a change below that key. Production builds still generate such patches, as v1 did, and still throw a `TypeError` for a symbol key. Keep the default array paths for such keys.

83.content: With `enableAutoFreeze`, development builds report a circular reference only for an object that holds itself. A changed draft that holds its original, as `draft.prev = original(draft)` makes it, or that links to a shared object through another path no longer throws; production builds always froze such states. For a real cycle, the error names the path of the object that repeats, which can be one key longer than in v1.

84.content: Development builds throw when a recipe passes a draft to the `set()` method of a Map draft, as in `draft.map.set(draft.key, value)`: Map keys are used as they are, so the next state would keep the draft as a key, revoked, and reading its properties would throw. Production builds still keep such a key, as v1 did. Use `original(draft)`, `current(draft)` or an id as the key.

85.content: `create()` with an explicit state type and an async recipe, such as `create<State>(base, async (draft) => { … })`, returns `Promise<State>`, and so do curried producers; v1 typed the result as `State`. A state type that is a type parameter, as in a generic function, or that includes Promises, such as `object` or `unknown`, still gives the state type for async recipes and for recipes that may return a Promise, as in v1; leave out the type argument in generic code.

86.content: `apply()` accepts `enableAutoFreeze: true` and then returns `Immutable<State>`, as `apply<State, true>()` does; v1 rejected the option and typed the frozen result as mutable. With `enableAutoFreeze` typed as `boolean` or optional `true`, the result is `State | Immutable<State>`. With `mutable` typed as `boolean`, optional `boolean`, or optional `true`, `apply()` returns `State | void`.

87.content: A curried producer whose recipe annotates its draft and returns a new state, such as `create((draft: State) => ({ ...draft, count: 0 }))`, returns `State`, or `Promise<State>` for an async recipe. v1 typed such a call as a manual draft, so calling the producer did not compile. A recipe whose draft is annotated with a type parameter, as in `create((draft: T) => { … })` in a generic function, also gives a producer, which v1 typed as a manual draft as well.

88.content: With an explicit state type, a recipe that may or may not return a Promise, such as one typed `(draft: State) => void | Promise<void>`, gives `State | Promise<State>`, also for a primitive state type, such as `number`, and in curried producers and creators from `makeCreator()`. v1 typed the result as `State`.

89.content: With `enablePatches`, every changed item of a Set keeps its changes. In v1, when two or more items of a Set that was not the root changed below their first level, the state kept the change of only one of them.

90.content: A Set that receives an unchanged draft holds the original object, as the rest of the state does, instead of the draft's shallow copy.

91.content: A Set draft that the recipe moves to another place, such as another key, an array, a Map, another Set or a new object, keeps its added, deleted and changed items there when its old place gets another value or is removed; v1 kept its original items.

92.content: A draft of a Set subclass changes its copy, an instance of the subclass, as Map drafts do: the subclass's own `add`, `has`, `delete` and `clear` take effect during the recipe, while the draft iterates the items in the order in which the Set holds them. v1 kept the items of a changed Set in a separate map, which bypassed those methods until it rebuilt the Set after the recipe. As a Map subclass's `set` already had to in v1, a Set subclass's `add` must store the value that it receives: an `add` that stores a copy of a draft, or of an object that holds drafts, leaves those drafts in the next state, where reading them throws.

93.content: Assigning `undefined` to a key that `delete`, `shift`, `unshift` or a shrinking `splice` removed from a draft adds the key back; v1 left a hole or kept the shorter length.

94.content: Under a `mark` that returns `mutable`, a value that the recipe assigned or moved is read back as assigned, through the draft and in `current()`; v1 returned the original value.

95.content: `current()` of a draft whose state holds a plain Set with drafts returns a snapshot; v1 threw.

96.content: `current()` snapshots an object that the recipe assigned and that `mark` makes draftable, such as a class instance, together with the drafts it holds; v1 returned the object as it was, so a later change to those drafts showed through the snapshot.

97.content: With `enableAutoFreeze`, Map and Set instances are frozen too, so adding a property or replacing a method fails as on any frozen object; v1 only replaced their mutators. Later producers skip a frozen Map or Set instead of walking its entries again, and a Map or Set that holds itself no longer overflows the stack in production builds.

98.content: The iterators that Map and Set drafts return behave like built-in iterators: iterating one that was partly consumed continues where it stopped, and iterator helpers such as `toArray()` are available where the engine has them. In v1, iterating such an iterator started over, and only a Map's `keys()` had the helpers.

99.content: Consume Map value and entry iterators, and all Set iterators, while their draft is active. After the producer finishes or fails, or a manual draft is finalized, an iterator cannot yield another value and throws a `TypeError`. Lazy iterator helpers follow the same lifetime; an exhausted iterator stays exhausted. Map keys are not drafted, and `keys()` continues to return a native iterator.

100.content: `apply()` copies the own symbol keys of patch values, and an own `__proto__` key, as `JSON.parse()` creates one, stays a data property. v1 dropped symbol keys there and turned an own `__proto__` key into the prototype of the copy.

101.content: `apply()` rejects a patch whose path ends in `__proto__` on an object or array, as it rejects `__proto__` earlier in a path. Coercible property keys, such as a boxed string, are checked after conversion too. With `mutable: true`, v1 assigned the value and so replaced the prototype of the object.

102.content: In a patch path, `apply()` reads an item of a Set only at its index, such as `1` or `'1'`, and throws for any other key, such as `__proto__`. v1 read any property of an array of the Set's items there, which let a path through `__proto__` reach `Array.prototype`.

103.content: `apply()` with `mutable: true` throws for a patch that replaces the root state with another value, such as the patch of a recipe that returns a new state, as the state cannot be replaced in place. v1 ignored the replacement and applied the patches after it to the replacing value, so the state stayed as it was and the value of that patch changed.

104.content: An object that `mark` makes draftable, such as a plain object under `markSimpleObject`, keeps an own `__proto__` key, as `JSON.parse()` creates one, as a property of its copy; v1 assigned it, which replaced the prototype of the copy.

105.content: A patch for a Map key that is an array holds the key as one path segment; v1 spread the array into the path, so applying the patch wrote to other keys.

106.content: `apply()` uses a Map key of a patch path as it is. v1 converted it to a string first, which threw for an object without a prototype.

107.content: Array patches record a change between `0` and `-0`, which the state already kept; in v1, applying the patches lost the sign. An element that stays `NaN` no longer yields a replace patch.

108.content: When a recipe shortens an array and lengthens it again, as `draft.length = 1; draft.length = 3` does, the patches replace the indices that the longer length exposes again. In v1, applying the patches kept the removed elements at those indices, and applying the inverse patches left holes there.

109.content: In strict mode, a nested `unsafe()` call no longer ends the access of the outer call; in v1, reading mutable data after it in the outer callback threw.

110.content: A producer that fails after its recipe returned, for example because the recipe changed the draft and returned another value, revokes its drafts and releases its array method cache, as a recipe that throws does; v1 left them usable. This also covers errors while inspecting a returned Proxy or calling a returned Promise's `then` method, and preserves the original error.

111.content: A draft of an array whose `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable` is false copies its elements; v1 put the whole array into the copy as its only element.

151.content: With the `enablePatches` option, `create()` also returns the patches that turn the base state into the next state, and the inverse patches that turn the next state back into the base state. `apply()` applies them, for example to replay changes on another copy of the state, to send them over a network, or to undo and redo changes.

152.content: `enablePatches` also works with curried producers, manual drafts and `makeCreator()`, and it supports objects, arrays, Maps, Sets, and the values that a `mark` makes draftable; pass the same `mark` to `apply()`.

153.content: **Operations and paths.** Patches use `add`, `remove` and `replace`. A path leads from the root to the changed value through object keys, array indices, Map keys as they are, objects and arrays included, and the positions of Set items. A recipe that returns a new state gets one `replace` patch with an empty path.

154.content: **Order.** The patches of a nested draft come before those of its parents, as in Immer.

155.content: **Values.** A patch value is the object that the next state holds, frozen with it when `enableAutoFreeze` is on, so copy a patch value before changing it. `apply()` copies patch values before applying them.

156.content: **Arrays.** `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()`, `reverse()` and `sort()` emit a `replace` patch for each index whose element changed, and an `add` patch for each index past the old length. An array that gets shorter gets one `replace` patch of its `length` by default, or a `remove` patch for each index it loses with `arrayLengthAssignment: false`. An array that a recipe shortens and lengthens again also gets patches for the indices that the longer length exposes again.

157.content: **Maps.** `set()` emits an `add` patch for a new key and a `replace` patch for an existing one, and `delete()` a `remove` patch.

158.content: **Sets.** Patches add an item by its value and remove one by the value it holds; see Sets of objects.

159.content: **Moved drafts.** A changed draft that leaves its key, because `sort()` or an assignment moved it or another value replaced it there, emits no patches under its old path; the patches of its parent carry its value.

160.content: **Applying patches.** `apply()` applies `add`, `remove` and `replace` patches and accepts `-` as the index that appends to an array. It throws for other operations and for paths through `__proto__` or `constructor`. It takes the `enableAutoFreeze`, `strict` and `mark` options, or `mutable: true` to change the state in place, which throws for a patch that replaces the root state with another value, and it changes a draft in place.

161.content: **JSON Patch.** With `pathAsArray: false` and `arrayLengthAssignment: false`, the patches of objects and arrays are JSON Patch operations. Maps and Sets have no JSON Patch counterpart.

170.content: Patches add a Set element by its value and remove one by the value it holds, so a `remove` patch removes an object only from a Set that holds that same object. A Set whose elements changed in place, without any element added or removed, gets patches under the position of each changed element, and they replay in both directions. Once a recipe adds or removes elements of a Set, the Set's `remove` and `add` patches carry every changed element by value instead. `apply()` copies the value of each patch before applying it, so a Set that `apply()` changes holds copies of the objects that patches add, and the inverse patches cannot remove those copies: an undo after a redo leaves the object in the Set. `apply()` also appends every element that it adds, so a Set that it changes can hold its elements in another order than the state that the recipe produced: a changed element of a Set that also added or removed elements, or an element that inverse patches add back, moves to the end, and a recipe that deletes an element and adds it back moves it to the end without a patch. The positions in the patches of a later recipe then find other elements, and its changes under them apply to another element without an error. Sets of primitives keep their elements, but their order can change in the same way. When patches are replayed on states that `apply()` returned, as undo, redo and synchronized copies do, keep such objects in a Map keyed by an id or in an array instead.

179.content: Mutative copies each object at most once per update and drafts only what a recipe reads, so most recipes are fast as they are. These tips help with large states and hot paths. The figures come from the benchmark on Node.js 24, in microseconds per update.

180.content: Every object that a recipe reads through a draft becomes a draft, so `draft.list.find()` creates a draft for each element it visits. Search `current(draft.list)`, which holds plain values, and change the match through the draft:

181.content: Updating the first of 10,000 rows and then finding and updating the last one took 176 µs this way and 2,169 µs through the draft. Take one snapshot for a series of searches: each call of `current()` copies the changed parts of the draft again. To read the base state without drafts, use `original()`.

182.content: Mutative searches a value that a recipe returns for drafts, which visits every object of it: returning a new state of 10,000 rows took 2,600 µs. When the value holds no drafts, such as a state built from scratch, wrap it in `rawReturn()`, which took 0.26 µs.

183.content: `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()` and `reverse()` run natively on the copy of a plain array, while a loop that moves elements one by one goes through the draft for each of them. Removing the first of 10,000 rows with `shift()` took 7.04 µs, against 7,408 µs for Immer, which moves each element through its draft. See which array methods run natively.

184.content: Each `create()` call copies the objects on the path from the root to its changes, so several changes in one recipe copy shared parents once, where one call per change copies them each time. Group the changes of an action or an event into one recipe.

185.content: **Auto-freeze** visits every object of the next state that is not frozen yet. Inserting a property into an object of 1,000 properties took 50.3 µs without it and 140 µs with it. Enable it in development, or where other code relies on frozen state; see Auto Freeze.

186.content: **Patches** cost little when an update changes a few paths: pushing a row and inserting a property at 10,000 rows took 63.8 µs without them and 63.2 µs with them. Moving elements emits a patch for each moved index, so removing the first of 10,000 rows took 1,063 µs with patches. Keep `arrayLengthAssignment` on unless the patches must be JSON Patch operations, since a `remove` patch per index costs more than one `replace` of the `length`.

187.content: **Strict mode** inspects every value that a recipe reads, and sends array methods and `current()` through the draft for arrays that may hold objects. Enable it in development only; see Strict Mode.

188.content: Data that recipes read but never change, such as a large lookup table in the state, is drafted object by object as recipes read it. Read it with `original()`, or keep it outside the state. A mark that returns `'mutable'` for it keeps it out of drafts altogether, but then a recipe that changes it changes it in place.

320.content: `create()` drafts a base state, runs a recipe that changes the draft, and returns the next state. The next state shares every part that the recipe left unchanged with the base state, and the base state itself does not change.

321.content: `base` is the state to draft: a plain object, an array, a `Map`, a `Set`, or a value that the `mark` option makes draftable, such as a class instance. Other objects, such as dates and class instances that no mark makes draftable, throw an error. With a recipe, a primitive or `null` base is passed to the recipe as it is, and the value that the recipe returns is the next state.

322.content: `recipe` receives the draft, and in a producer also the other arguments of the producer. It changes the draft and returns nothing, or returns a new state. It can be an async function.

With `enablePatches`, it returns `[nextState, patches, inversePatches]`: the patches turn the base state into the next state, and the inverse patches turn it back. For an async recipe, it returns a Promise of either.

A string path holds only strings, so it cannot name a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key: with `pathAsArray: false`, the patch of `draft.set(1, 'b')` would set the key `'1'`. An instance that `mark` makes `immutable` is copied with all its own properties, and those that are enumerable, writable and configurable are assigned, so an own property that shadows a setter of its class runs it, and one that shadows a getter or a read-only property throws; see Copying marked instances.

436.content: That search visits every object of the returned value, which takes time for large values. `rawReturn()` skips it for a value that holds no drafts, such as a state built from scratch or an earlier state:

Replace such values, as the recipe above replaces `updatedAt`, or mark their class as `immutable` so that Mutative drafts and copies them.

452.content: Every difference between Mutative and Immer 11.1.18 in APIs, defaults, drafts and patches, and the behaviors that both share.

460.content: Mutative and Immer work the same way: a recipe changes a draft, and the library produces the next state, which shares every part that the recipe left unchanged. Most code moves from Immer by renaming its functions, as the migration guide shows. This page lists the differences that change what code does or produces, checked against Immer 11.1.18, and the behaviors that both libraries share where it is easy to assume otherwise.

530.content: **Auto-freeze.** Mutative leaves results unfrozen unless `enableAutoFreeze` is set, while Immer freezes them by default. With freezing on, both freeze the whole result deeply, unchanged parts included, and freeze Map and Set instances so that their mutators throw. Mutative also freezes the objects that a Map uses as keys, which Immer leaves unfrozen.

531.content: **Options per call.** Each `create()` and `apply()` call takes its own options, and `makeCreator()` sets defaults, where Immer's `setAutoFreeze()` and its plugins change the module for every caller. Maps, Sets and patches work without the `enableMapSet()` and `enablePatches()` calls that Immer requires and throws without.

532.content: **Marking.** A `mark` function decides how values are drafted: it can make class instances draftable without changing their class, where Immer requires an `[immerable]` property on it, keep values mutable so that the recipe changes them in place, or return a function that copies a value. Mutative copies a class instance that a mark makes draftable with all its own properties, non-enumerable ones included, as Immer does with `setUseStrictShallowCopy('class_only')`, but assigns those that are enumerable, writable and configurable, as Immer's default copy does, so an own property that shadows a setter of the class runs it; see Copying marked instances. Both copy only the enumerable properties of plain objects and read their getters as values. See mark.

533.content: **Strict mode.** With `strict: true`, reading a value that the recipe could change without a draft, such as a class instance that is not marked, throws unless the read happens inside `unsafe()`. Immer has no such mode. See strict mode.

534.content: **Map and Set subclasses** keep their class and its methods, in drafts and in the next state. Immer's next state holds plain Maps and Sets instead.

535.content: **ES2025 Set methods**, such as `union()` and `isSubsetOf()`, work on Set drafts and compare objects as iterating the draft returns them; see the FAQ. On Immer's Set drafts they do not see the draft's items: `union()` of a draft of `new Set([1, 2])` with `new Set([3])` returns `Set {3}`.

536.content: **Async recipes** make `create()` return a Promise of the result, and the draft stays usable until the Promise settles; see create(). Immer 11 throws, because the returned Promise counts as a new value while the recipe changed the draft.

537.content: **A draft passed to a nested `create()`** is copied, where Immer's `produce()` drafts the draft itself; see create() on a draft.

538.content: **Returned values.** Both replace the state with a value that the recipe returns, and both throw when the recipe also changed the draft. `rawReturn()` returns `undefined`, as Immer's `nothing` does, and also returns a value without searching it for drafts; see rawReturn().

539.content: **Array methods.** `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()` and `reverse()` move the elements of a plain array on its copy, and `indexOf()`, `lastIndexOf()` and `includes()` search it natively, under the contract that the FAQ describes. Immer runs them through the proxy unless its opt-in `enableArrayMethods()` plugin is enabled, which in Immer 11.1.18 can return raw base objects and emit patches that fail to replay; see the audit.

540.content: **Alike in both.** Each path to a shared object gets its own draft; see shared references. A class instance that is neither marked nor `[immerable]` is not drafted, so a recipe that changes it changes the base state. `current()` and `original()` throw for values that are not drafts. An iteration over a Map draft that starts before the recipe changes the Map walks the base Map, in both libraries; see the FAQ.

541.content: Both libraries emit the same patches for most changes: the same operations, paths and values, the patches of nested drafts before those of their parents, and values that are the objects of the next state, frozen with it when freezing is on. They differ in the following cases; Patches describes how Mutative generates and applies them.

542.content: **Arrays that get shorter.** By default, Mutative records a shorter array with a `replace` patch of its `length`, as in the patches of `pop()` and `list.length = 0` and in the inverse patches of `push()` and of a `splice()` that inserts, while Immer removes each index with a `remove` patch. With `enablePatches: { arrayLengthAssignment: false }`, Mutative emits the same `remove` patches as Immer.

543.content: **Changed items of a Set.** When a recipe changes objects in a Set without adding or removing items, Mutative emits a `replace` patch under the position of each changed item, while Immer removes the old object and adds the new one. Once the recipe adds or removes items, both carry the changed items by value.

544.content: **String paths.** With `enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }`, Mutative emits paths as JSON Pointer strings, as JSON Patch requires, while Immer's paths are always arrays. A string path cannot name a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key.

545.content: **Applying patches.** `apply()` takes the `enableAutoFreeze`, `strict` and `mark` options, or `mutable: true` to change the state in place and return `undefined`.

546.content: **Alike in both.** `apply()` and `applyPatches()` change a draft in place, copy patch values before applying them, accept `-` as the index that appends to an array, and reject `move`, `copy` and `test` operations and paths through `__proto__` or `constructor`. As they copy patch values, an object that patches add to a Set is a copy, which the inverse patches cannot remove, so an undo after a redo leaves it in the Set in both libraries, and both append the elements that patches add, so such a Set can hold its elements in another order; see Sets of objects.

547.content: Mutative passes the test suite of Immer, adapted to its API. The non-support tests pin cases that Immer 11.1.18 gets wrong and Mutative does not, such as a draft that escapes into the next state and Map keys that stay mutable after freezing. The array methods audit reproduces patch ordering, base mutation and draft finalization failures of Immer's `enableArrayMethods()` plugin, with reproduction tests that include plugin-disabled controls and run the same recipes against Mutative.

548.content: With matched settings, both freezing or both not and both generating patches or both not, Mutative was faster than Immer 11.1.18 in 595 of 614 measured cases, 3.6x on geometric mean. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases, 6.6x on geometric mean. Immer was faster only with auto-freeze: when updating class instances with many fields, and in two 100-row array updates whose runs overlapped those of Mutative.

549.content: With patches on and auto-freeze off, Mutative was faster in 148 of 150 cases and never slower, and faster in every array case: 4.4x Immer and 13x Mutative 1.3.0 on geometric mean. The comparisons run Immer without its `enableArrayMethods()` plugin. In Immer 11.1.18 the plugin returns raw base objects from `shift`, `pop` and `splice`, so editing them changes the previous state, and its patches can fail to replay; the audit above reproduces these failures.

702.content: Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes, drafts only the values that a recipe reads, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and moves array elements natively on its copies instead of through the draft's proxy. It also leaves the next state unfrozen by default. See Performance for the measurements.

703.content: Yes. Unless you have to be compatible with Internet Explorer, Mutative supports almost all of Immer's features, and the migration guide shows how to replace each API. Comparison with Immer lists the APIs that replace Immer's and every behavior that differs.

704.content: Mutative, like Immer, needs `Proxy`. On Android, React Native supports it since version 0.59 with JavaScriptCore and since version 0.64 with Hermes.

705.content: Yes. A producer with an action argument is a reducer, and a recipe can return a new state, for example the initial state with `rawReturn()`. Redux Toolkit drafts state with Immer in `createSlice()` and `createReducer()`, and an RFC to make its `produce()` configurable is open.

706.content: `shift`, `unshift`, `splice` and `reverse` move elements directly on the copy of a plain array without holes, including `undefined` elements; `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf` and `includes` search the current array natively; `sort` and `join` run natively on arrays of primitives. Removed elements are returned as drafts, patches replay in both directions, and a call that changes nothing keeps the state. Sparse arrays, array subclasses, an own `constructor` or `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable`, arrays under a custom `mark`, every method with a callback, `at`, `slice`, `fill` and `copyWithin` use the proxy path. An argument that can run user code, such as an object passed as `fromIndex` or as a `splice` index, is converted on the proxy path, so a conversion that changes the array is observed as the native methods observe it. The fast paths are made for data arrays: an accessor property defined on an array index is read as a data value, and the number and order of such getter calls, their re-entrant effects on the draft, and the identity of objects they return are not guaranteed to match element-by-element execution through the proxy. With auto-freeze, Mutative may also read such a getter twice when it copies a frozen, sealed or non-extensible array.

707.content: Optimized searches give the same results as the proxy path, comparing elements as a read returns them. Drafts, values assigned in the recipe, non-draftable objects and primitives are found. An object of the base state is drafted when it is read, so it is never found, whether or not it was read before, unless the recipe assigned or inserted it and it is not at its original index; use `original()` to search the base state, for example `original(draft.list).indexOf(item)`. The search never reads a property of the value it is given.

708.content: In strict mode, outside `unsafe()`, optimized calls on an array that may hold objects take the proxy path unchanged, so reading a non-draftable element fails exactly as it always did; arrays of primitives, recognized with `typeof` alone, keep the native paths. Elements are moved and compared without being inspected, while the proxy path inspects each element it reads. An element that is itself a Proxy may therefore see fewer calls to its internal methods on the native paths, never more and never at other times; a revoked Proxy element that a search passes over, for example, does not throw there.

709.content: Draftable base elements removed or moved by these methods are drafted before they are exposed. Methods with callbacks, such as `forEach`, `map`, `filter` and `find`, go through the draft so that their callbacks see every change and can modify elements; use `current()` for read-only scans of large arrays.

710.content: Yes. Deleting the entry being visited and changing the values of other entries work as on a Map, and Set drafts iterate like Sets. One difference remains: an iteration over a Map draft that starts before the recipe has changed that Map, or read an object value from it, walks the entries of the base Map. An entry that the recipe deletes later in such an iteration is still visited, with `undefined` as its value, and an entry that it adds is not visited. To delete other entries while iterating, iterate over `Array.from(draft.keys())` and skip the keys for which `draft.has()` returns false.

711.content: Yes, but they compare elements as iterating the draft returns them. An object of the base state is a draft there, so these methods do not match it with the original object, although `has()` accepts the original object. To compare a Set draft with objects of the base state, call the method on `current(draft)`, in which unchanged objects keep their identity, or on `original(draft)` for the base state, or compare ids, for example `[...draft].filter((item) => ids.has(item.id))`. This applies to `union()`, `intersection()`, `difference()`, `symmetricDifference()`, `isSubsetOf()`, `isSupersetOf()` and `isDisjointFrom()`.

712.content: No. Map keys are used as they are, and a draft is revoked when its producer ends, so a Map that kept a draft as a key, and the patches that name that key, would hold a revoked draft, whose properties throw when they are read. Use `original(draft)`, `current(draft)` or an id as the key. Development builds throw when a recipe passes a draft to the `set()` method of a Map draft.

713.content: Yes, Mutative supports shared references, but **each path to a shared object gets its own independent draft**. Modifications to one path do not automatically reflect in others. If you want to preserve shared references in the result, you must explicitly assign them (e.g., `draft.b = draft.a`). Read more details.

714.content: No. Mutative revokes the drafts of a `create()` call when its recipe ends, also when it fails, so reading a draft afterwards throws. Keep `current(draft)`, a snapshot of plain values, or the next state instead. A draft of a manual `create(base)` lives until `finalize()` returns, and the draft of an async recipe until its Promise settles.

742.content: How Mutative drafts an object that several paths of the state lead to, and how to keep it shared.

746.content: Mutative supports non-unidirectional trees (DAGs with shared nodes) where there is more than one path from the root to the same node, **as long as there are no cycles**. However, there is an important behavior to understand regarding how drafts handle these shared references.

747.content: When the same object is referenced from multiple paths in the base state, Mutative creates **independent drafts for each path**. This means modifications to one path will **not** automatically reflect in the other paths.

748.content: This behavior is **by design** and matches Immer's behavior. Each path through the state tree gets its own independent draft proxy.

749.content: If you need to **preserve or create shared references** in the result state, you must do so explicitly within your recipe function by assigning one draft to another.

753.content: Each path gets its own **independent draft**. Mutations through one path do **not** reflect in other paths.

755.content: ✅ **Supported**. Assigning `draft.x = draft.y` creates shared references in the final state.

757.content: ❌ **Not supported**. Cycles are actively detected in development mode when auto-freeze is enabled.

782.content: Drafts, finalization with structural sharing, patches and marks, the ideas behind Mutative.

788.content: Mutative is based on `Proxy`. A recipe changes a draft of the state, Mutative records which parts changed, and it produces the next state from those changes, sharing every part that did not change. Patches describe the changes, and marks decide which values are drafted.

789.content: The current state is the base state, which never changes.

790.content: The draft is where the recipe makes its changes. Mutative creates a draft of each object that the recipe reads, shown with dotted lines, and copies the objects that it changes, shown in red.

791.content: The next state holds the copies of the changed objects and shares all the others with the base state.

792.content: A draft is a `Proxy` of a value of the state. It behaves like that value: a recipe reads it, assigns to it, deletes from it and calls its methods, such as `push()` on arrays or `set()` on Maps. Mutative drafts lazily:

793.content: Reading a draftable value through a draft gives a draft of it, created on that first read. Plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets are draftable, and so are the values that a mark makes draftable, such as class instances; see `isDraftable()`. Other values, such as primitives and dates, are returned as they are.

794.content: The first change to a draft makes a shallow copy of its value, and later changes go to the same copy, so Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes the recipe makes.

795.content: Values that the recipe assigns are not drafted: the next state holds them as they are.

796.content: Each path to an object gets a draft of its own, also when several paths lead to the same object; see Shared references.

797.content: Drafts live only as long as their `create()` call: when the recipe ends, Mutative revokes them, and reading one later throws. Keep `current(draft)`, a snapshot of plain values, instead of a draft, and check for drafts with `isDraft()`.

798.content: When the recipe ends, Mutative finalizes the drafts: the next state holds the copy of each changed draft and the original value of every unchanged one, so it shares every object that the recipe did not change with the base state. A recipe that changes nothing returns the base state itself. With auto-freeze, Mutative then freezes the next state deeply.

799.content: A recipe can also return a new state instead of changing the draft; see Returning a new state.

800.content: With the `enablePatches` option, `create()` also returns patches, which describe the changes of the recipe, and inverse patches, which undo them. Each patch is an object with an `op`, `add`, `remove` or `replace`, a `path` from the root to the changed value, and, for `add` and `replace`, the new `value`. `apply()` applies patches to a state, for example to replay changes on another copy of the state or to undo them; see Patches.

801.content: A state can mix data that should be drafted with data that should not, such as class instances, caches or values from other libraries. The `mark` option decides, value by value, whether Mutative drafts a value, leaves it mutable, or copies it with a function of your own, without marking the objects themselves. See Marking data structure.

**Arrays.** `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()`, `reverse()` and `sort()` emit a `replace` patch for each index whose element changed, and an `add` patch for each index past the old length. An array that gets shorter gets one `replace` patch of its `length` by default, or a `remove` patch for each index it loses with `arrayLengthAssignment: false`. **Order.** The patches of a nested draft now come before those of its parents, the order Immer uses. For example, `const item = draft.list[0]; draft.list.length = 0; item.text = 'b'; draft.item = item;` yields the `list` length replace before the `item` add. Patches add a Set element by its value and remove one by the value it holds, so a `remove` patch removes an object only from a Set that holds that same object. A Set whose elements changed in place, without any element added or removed, gets patches under the position of each changed element, and they replay in both directions. Once a recipe adds or removes elements of a Set, the Set's `remove` and `add` patches carry every changed element by value instead. `apply()` copies the value of each patch before applying it, so a Set that `apply()` changes holds copies of the objects that patches add, and the inverse patches cannot remove those copies: an undo after a redo leaves the object in the Set. `apply()` also appends every element that it adds, so a Set that it changes can hold its elements in another order than the state that the recipe produced: a changed element of a Set that also added or removed elements, or an element that inverse patches add back, moves to the end, and a recipe that deletes an element and adds it back moves it to the end without a patch. The positions in the patches of a later recipe then find other elements, and its changes under them apply to another element without an error. Sets of primitives keep their elements, but their order can change in the same way.
